clue.text: How you might find some stands in the park, if really wild!

definitions.text: How you might find some stands in the park
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a bandstand in a park is a stand that has a band on it
second meaning: done with total lack of restraint

explanation.surface: Someone describing where to find stands in a park, if the place has gone thoroughly feral.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as WITH A BAND ON and it describes a bandstand, the covered platform where a band plays in a park; read as two words it means wildly, without restraint.
explanation.definitionFit: To act 'with abandon' is an idiom for acting with complete, uninhibited freedom, which is what really wild behaviour is.

clue.text: A philosopher who could show another philosopher how to start his will.

parts.note: a will traditionally opens 'I, (name)...', so the testator begins with the letter I
Socrates, the Athenian philosopher

explanation.surface: One thinker who could teach a fellow thinker the correct way to begin drafting his last testament.
explanation.walkthrough: A will starts 'I, Socrates...', so I followed by the name of the other philosopher gives the answer. Isocrates was an Athenian orator and teacher of rhetoric, a contemporary of Plato.
explanation.definitionFit: Isocrates ran a famous school in Athens and is counted among the classical Greek thinkers, so he qualifies as a philosopher.

clue.text: Praise be! (Has on an otherwise different appearance, too!)

indicators.note: giving the letters a different appearance means rearranging them into another word

explanation.surface: An exclamation of praise, with a bracketed aside about someone wearing something that changes how they look.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosanna is a shout of praise or adoration to God, used in Christian worship much like 'Praise be!'

clue.text: They were smiling at me in tune.

definitions.text: They were smiling at me in tune.

parts.words: They were smiling at me in tune
parts.note: an allusion to the Irving Berlin song whose opening line has the sky smiling down at the singer

explanation.walkthrough: 'In tune' means in a song: Irving Berlin's standard opens 'Blue skies, smiling at me, nothing but blue skies do I see'.
explanation.definitionFit: The things smiling at the singer in that famous lyric are cloudless heavens, named in its first two words.

clue.text: If confused, infer it from a rather slangy description of the more worthwhile.

definitions.text: a rather slangy description of the more worthwhile

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are mixed up, as in a confused order

explanation.surface: If muddled, you might deduce something from a slang term for the better option.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Infer' looks like an instruction to deduce, but 'confused' says the letters of INFER IT are to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Nifty is informal for good or smart, so its comparative is a casual way of calling something better or more worthwhile.

clue.text: A place not far from Salt Lake where you get to go up to study.

definitions.text: A place not far from Salt Lake

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written before it is turned round
a den is a private room for working or reading, a study

explanation.surface: A town near Salt Lake where one can head off to university.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'up' means the word go is written from the bottom, giving OG. Ogden is a city in Utah, about 35 miles north of Salt Lake City.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogden sits on the Wasatch Front just north of Salt Lake City, so it is a nearby place.

clue.text: Taking a public vote ends up with nothing, according to the old god.

indicators.note: the next piece is placed at the end, after what comes before

parts.note: a poll is a vote or survey of the public
O, the round figure zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: Holding a ballot produces no result, according to an ancient deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollo was a Greek and Roman god of the sun, music and prophecy, a deity of antiquity.

clue.text: It once meant skillful–now it has a more sly meaning.

definitions.text: It once meant skillful–now it has a more sly meaning.

parts.words: It once meant skillful–now it has a more sly meaning
parts.note: describes a word's history: in older English it meant skilled in a craft, today it means cunning

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a potted word history. In Old and Middle English the word meant strong or skilful, from 'craft' meaning skill; its modern sense is wily.
explanation.definitionFit: Its sense shifted from skilled at a trade to cunning or deceitful, exactly the move the clue describes.

clue.text: First class, as Fido might get to sniff things out.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: meeting the required standard, excellent

definitions.text: as Fido might get to sniff things out
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: a dog going ..., that is to sniff, something

explanation.walkthrough: Fido is a stock name for a pet dog, and snuff in its old sense means to sniff or inhale through the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something meeting the expected standard, hence of good or first-class quality.

clue.text: See 9
The thing the unknowing are in.

definitions.text: The thing the unknowing are in.

parts.words: The thing the unknowing are in
parts.note: people who know nothing about a matter are said to be 'in the' something

explanation.walkthrough: The clue points at the idiom for not being informed: someone who knows nothing is kept in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Being 'in the dark' is an idiom for being uninformed, so it is the state the unknowing are in.

clue.text: Foreign money found in most of Florida, and a couple of other points.

indicators.note: only most of the state's name is used, so its ending is dropped

parts.note: N and S, the compass points north and south

explanation.surface: Overseas currency turning up in most of the Sunshine State and at a couple of other spots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' here drops two letters, leaving FLORI; then two compass points finish it.
explanation.definitionFit: The florin was a coin of Florence, later of the Netherlands and other countries, so florins are a foreign currency to an American reader.

clue.text: Mean! Ink, as they say, if your head is tacked on.

indicators.note: the following piece is attached at the end of what comes before

parts.note: to ink a deal is slang for signing it

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: Y is the first letter of your

explanation.surface: Someone exclaiming about stinginess and ink, once a head is nailed into place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean!' looks like an exclamation about stinginess, but it is the verb meaning to denote. SIGN and IF come first, and 'your head' (its first letter Y) 'is tacked on' at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To signify something is to stand for or express it, which is what a word does when it means something.

clue.text: See 4
The better type might be found here, to closely follow what the train is on.

definitions.text: The better type might be found here

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely
a train runs on a track of rails

explanation.surface: The superior sort can be found here, tailing whatever the railway carriage runs on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like the comparative of good, but here it is one who bets, the punter at a greyhound race.
explanation.definitionFit: Greyhound racing venues are places where gamblers gather to place wagers on the dogs.

clue.text: Concerning old songs and poetry, you might find them on the last part of 15.

definitions.text: you might find them on the last part of 15

parts.note: re means about or concerning
lays are old narrative songs or poems

explanation.surface: Something about old ballads and verse, and where you might find them at the end of an earlier answer.
explanation.walkthrough: The last part of 15 across is TRACK, and relay races are run on a track.
explanation.definitionFit: Relays are team races in which runners hand over a baton, and they are run on an athletics track.

clue.text: Could be either the man or the machine, but the sward is all the better for it.

definitions.text: Could be either the man or the machine, but the sward is all the better for it.

parts.words: Could be either the man or the machine, but the sward is all the better for it
parts.note: the word names both the person cutting grass and the device that cuts it, and either leaves the turf neater

explanation.walkthrough: A sward is an expanse of short grass; the answer can mean the gardener doing the cutting or the machine he pushes.
explanation.definitionFit: The term is used both for the grass-cutting machine and for a person who cuts grass, and either improves a lawn.

clue.text: The song comes back to be with mystical knowledge.

indicators.note: coming back means the word is read in the return direction, from its end

parts.note: taken as written before it is turned round
is is a form of the verb to be

explanation.surface: A tune returns, carrying some esoteric wisdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnosis, from the Greek for knowledge, is spiritual or esoteric insight of the kind the Gnostics claimed.

clue.text: Gave out the rumor that it could be onside?

indicators.note: the letters could be arranged as another word, a sign to rearrange them

explanation.surface: Someone spread word that a player might not be offside after all.
explanation.walkthrough: Onside is a sports term for a player in a legal position; 'could be' says its letters could be rearranged into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To noise something abroad is an old phrase for spreading a report, so noised means gave out a rumour.

clue.text: Title given the little company up and down–but it's just a big blow!

parts.note: Sir is the title given to a knight
CO, the short form of company, read once upwards and once downwards in this down entry

explanation.surface: A small firm is honoured with a knighthood up and down, yet it is all hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: CO, the abbreviation for company, appears twice: first going up (OC), then going down (CO).
explanation.definitionFit: A sirocco is a hot, dusty wind blowing from North Africa across the Mediterranean, so a strong wind.

clue.text: How you sometimes can't get a word in, if knowledgeable about the slight advantage.

definitions.text: How you sometimes can't get a word in

indicators.note: wise about the edge reads as a compound in which the thing one is wise about comes first

parts.note: an edge is a small advantage over rivals
wise means knowledgeable

explanation.surface: Sometimes you can't interrupt someone who knows all about having a narrow lead.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse reads like a compound such as streetwise: wise about the edge, with the edge put first.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'can't get a word in edgewise' describes being unable to speak because someone else talks nonstop.

clue.text: Could be associated with Moses, and a slangy note hurried crazy-mad to make it!

parts.note: a G, short for grand, is slang for a thousand-dollar note
ran means hurried

indicators.note: the letters of the next word are sent crazy, that is scrambled

explanation.surface: Something linked to Moses, made from cash slang, rushing and lunacy.
explanation.walkthrough: Moses here is Grandma Moses, the American folk painter, not the biblical prophet; 'crazy' jumbles the word mad into DMA.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna Mary Robertson Moses became famous as Grandma Moses, so the word is attached to her name.

clue.text: A point in your extra wheel covering could be rather hard to find.

definitions.text: could be rather hard to find

indicators.note: the point goes inside the other piece

parts.note: the spare is the extra tire carried for a wheel
S, the compass point south

explanation.surface: A point in your spare tire may well be tricky to locate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A point' suggests a puncture in the tire, but it is a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sparse is thinly scattered or scarce, so it can be hard to come by.

clue.text: The one of Samothrace celebrated such winning ways when the old theatre troupe gets conservative.

definitions.text: The one of Samothrace celebrated such winning ways

parts.note: the Old Vic, a historic London theatre and its company, known as the Vic
a Tory is a member of the British Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A famous statue honoured success, just as an old acting company turns right-wing.
explanation.walkthrough: The Old Vic is a London theatre; its company is the Vic. The Winged Victory of Samothrace is a Greek statue in the Louvre.
explanation.definitionFit: The statue known as the Winged Victory of Samothrace commemorates a naval triumph, the success of winning ways.

clue.text: Possibly stale output from a physicist and inventor.

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters may be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Perhaps a scientist's work has gone stale.
explanation.definitionFit: Nikola Tesla was the Serbian-American engineer and physicist behind alternating-current systems and many inventions.

clue.text: He who founded the city of Thebes was a low-down scoundrel, and real nasty!

definitions.text: He who founded the city of Thebes
definitions.note: the answer is the adjective from that founder's name, so the definition stands for 'of him'

parts.note: a cad is a dishonourable man
mean means unkind or nasty

explanation.surface: The founder of Thebes is revealed as a cheat and a truly unpleasant man.
explanation.walkthrough: Cadmus founded Thebes in Greek myth; the answer is the adjective from his name, so the definition is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadmean means relating to Cadmus, the mythical Phoenician prince who founded Thebes.

clue.text: Were wrong, but could hold water.

indicators.note: the letters are put into a wrong order, that is rearranged

explanation.surface: People were mistaken, but their argument might still hold water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold water' sounds like the idiom for a sound argument; here it is literal, and 'wrong' says the letters of WERE are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewer is a large jug or pitcher, a vessel for carrying water.

clue.text: They really get turned on as a team!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: gas ... or water ..., which are turned on
second meaning: the New York ..., an American football team

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests excited fans; the two halves are separate meanings, gas or water jets and the NFL team.
explanation.definitionFit: Jets are nozzles that spray gas or water when opened, and the Jets are a professional football franchise.

clue.text: Intimidated to marry each other?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: wedded together, joint marriage

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful reading: split as CO-WED, the word suggests two people wed jointly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone cowed has been daunted or browbeaten into submission, which is to be intimidated.

clue.text: If you're worried about something, they say everything will come out in it, according to Shaw, possibly.

definitions.text: If you're worried about something, they say everything will come out in it

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of the name may be rearranged

explanation.surface: Reassurance for worriers, attributed perhaps to George Bernard Shaw.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying is 'it'll all come out in the wash'; Shaw is not the source, and 'possibly' says his name's letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb means problems sort themselves out eventually, as stains come out in the laundry.

clue.text: Knowing what to do in Paris?

definitions.text: Knowing what to do in Paris?

parts.words: Knowing what to do in Paris
parts.note: the French phrase literally means knowing how to do, as it would be said in Paris

explanation.walkthrough: The French phrase translates as 'to know how to do', so it is how a Parisian would say knowing what to do.
explanation.definitionFit: English borrowed the French expression for social poise: the knack of acting appropriately in any situation.
